title: ISS626-VAA
text:
Welcome to ISS626 Visual Analytics and Applications. In this website, you will find my coursework prepared for this course
The first hands-on exercise is split into two linked parts. Exercise 1A focuses on importing and processing Singapore geospatial data, while Exercise 1B uses the prepared data for thematic mapping and geo-visualisation.

Exercise 1A: Geospatial Data Science
Exercise 1B: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation

title: Hands-on Exercise 1A: Geospatial Data Science with R
text:
This exercise follows the first chapter of the course workbook. I used the current public releases where possible, then worked through the same core ideas: importing several geometry types, checking the coordinate reference system (CRS), bringing all layers into SVY21, and using spatial operations to answer small planning questions.
Before rendering the page, run Rscript scripts/download_data.R from the project root. The raw-data sources and the reason for using the current GeoJSON releases are recorded in the data-provenance note.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1A: Geospatial Data Science with R
text:
Importing the layers
The subzone boundary is a polygon layer, cycling paths are line features, and pre-schools are point features. All three files arrive in WGS84, so I transform them to SVY21 (EPSG:3414) immediately. This makes later buffering and area calculations meaningful in metres.


Show R code
mpsz <- st_read(file.path(geo_dir, "masterplan_subzones.geojson"), quiet = TRUE) |>
  st_transform(3414)

cyclingpath <- st_read(file.path(geo_dir, "cycling_paths.geojson"), quiet = TRUE) |>
  st_transform(3414)

preschool <- st_read(file.path(geo_dir, "preschools.geojson"), quiet = TRUE) |>
  st_transform(3414)

tibble(
  layer = c("Planning subzones", "Cycling paths", "Pre-schools"),
  features = c(nrow(mpsz), nrow(cyclingpath), nrow(preschool)),
  geometry = c(as.character(st_geometry_type(mpsz)[1]),
               as.character(st_geometry_type(cyclingpath)[1]),
               as.character(st_geometry_type(preschool)[1]))
)

A quick spatial check
The first plot is deliberately simple. It is useful for checking that the boundary and points are drawing in the same place before moving to a more polished map.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1A: Geospatial Data Science with R
section: Converting an aspatial table into points
text:
Converting an aspatial table into points
Inside Airbnb supplies a regular CSV, but it contains longitude and latitude. After checking for missing coordinates, st_as_sf() converts the table into points and st_transform() puts it into the same CRS as the other layers.


Show R code
listings <- read_csv(file.path(asp_dir, "singapore_listings.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(!is.na(longitude), !is.na(latitude))

listings_sf <- st_as_sf(listings, coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326) |>
  st_transform(3414)

title: Hands-on Exercise 1A: Geospatial Data Science with R
text:
Buffering cycling paths
For a manageable local example, I selected cycling paths that meet Tampines West and added a 5-metre buffer. Working in SVY21 matters here: a five-unit buffer is now a five-metre buffer, not five decimal degrees.


Show R code
tampines_west <- mpsz |> filter(SUBZONE_N == "TAMPINES WEST")
cycling_tampines <- st_filter(cyclingpath, tampines_west)
cycling_buffer <- st_buffer(cycling_tampines, dist = 5)

buffer_area_m2 <- sum(st_area(cycling_buffer))
buffer_area_m2


119453.6 [m^2]




Show R code
plot(st_geometry(tampines_west), col = "grey95", border = "grey35", main = "Five-metre cycling-path buffer in Tampines West")
plot(st_geometry(cycling_buffer), add = TRUE, col = rgb(0.2, 0.6, 0.8, 0.35), border = NA)
plot(st_geometry(cycling_tampines), add = TRUE, col = "#176b87", lwd = 0.8)









The displayed area is a sum of feature buffers, so overlapping buffer sections can be counted more than once. That is acceptable for demonstrating the operation; a land-acquisition estimate would dissolve overlapping buffers first.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1A: Geospatial Data Science with R
text:
Counting pre-schools by subzone
st_intersects() returns the pre-school points that fall inside each subzone. Counting those matches and dividing by the polygon area gives both an absolute count and a comparable density.


Show R code
mpsz_preschools <- mpsz |>
  mutate(
    preschool_count = lengths(st_intersects(mpsz, preschool)),
    area_km2 = as.numeric(st_area(geometry)) / 1e6,
    preschool_density = preschool_count / area_km2
  )

mpsz_preschools |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(SUBZONE_N, PLN_AREA_N, preschool_count, preschool_density) |>
  arrange(desc(preschool_count)) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)

Show R code
ggplot(mpsz_preschools, aes(x = preschool_density)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 24, fill = "#62a8ac", colour = "white") +
  labs(
    title = "Pre-school density is uneven across subzones",
    x = "Pre-schools per square kilometre",
    y = "Number of subzones"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()









The histogram makes a useful distinction: a large subzone can have many centres but still have moderate density, while a compact residential subzone can stand out once area is taken into account. That is why both measures are worth keeping.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1B: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation
text:
This page extends Exercise 1A by joining a resident-population table to planning subzones and mapping the result. The focus is not just on making a coloured map: the classifications, palette, and supporting chart all change what is easy to notice.
The population table covers 2011–2020, so I use 2020 as the last available year. The public data sources and download instructions are listed in the data-provenance note.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1B: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation
text:
This page extends Exercise 1A by joining a resident-population table to planning subzones and mapping the result. The focus is not just on making a coloured map: the classifications, palette, and supporting chart all change what is easy to notice.
The population table covers 2011–2020, so I use 2020 as the last available year. The public data sources and download instructions are listed in the data-provenance note.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1B: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation
text:
Preparing the demographic table
The source table is disaggregated by sex and dwelling type, so I sum those rows first. I then group the age bands into young residents (0–24), economically active residents (25–64), and older residents (65 and above). The dependency ratio is the combined young and older population divided by the economically active population.


Show R code
popdata <- read_csv(file.path(asp_dir, "respopagesextod2011to2020.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)

young_ages <- c("0_to_4", "5_to_9", "10_to_14", "15_to_19", "20_to_24")
active_ages <- c("25_to_29", "30_to_34", "35_to_39", "40_to_44", "45_to_49", "50_to_54", "55_to_59", "60_to_64")

population_2020 <- popdata |>
  filter(Time == 2020) |>
  mutate(
    cohort = case_when(
      AG %in% young_ages ~ "young",
      AG %in% active_ages ~ "active",
      TRUE ~ "aged"
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(PA, SZ, cohort) |>
  summarise(population = sum(Pop), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = cohort, values_from = population, values_fill = 0) |>
  mutate(
    total = young + active + aged,
    dependency = if_else(active > 0, (young + aged) / active, NA_real_),
    PA = str_to_upper(PA),
    SZ = str_to_upper(SZ)
  )

population_2020

title: Hands-on Exercise 1B: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation
Hands-on Exercise 1B: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation
text:
A first choropleth map


Show R code
dependency_map <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "dependency",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 5, values = "YlOrRd"),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Dependency ratio"),
    col = "white",
    lwd = 0.15
  ) +
  tm_title("Resident dependency ratio by planning subzone, 2020") +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE)

dependency_map









Quantiles make the visual emphasis relative: each class contains a similar number of subzones. That is useful when looking for a ranking, but it should not be read as equally sized differences in the underlying ratio.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1B: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation
text:
Comparing classifications and palettes


Show R code
equal_map <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "dependency", fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "equal", n = 5, values = "Blues"), col = "white", lwd = 0.1) +
  tm_title("Equal intervals")

quantile_map <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "dependency", fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 5, values = "YlOrRd"), col = "white", lwd = 0.1) +
  tm_title("Quantiles")

jenks_map <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "dependency", fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "fisher", n = 5, values = "Purples"), col = "white", lwd = 0.1) +
  tm_title("Fisher-Jenks")

tmap_arrange(equal_map, quantile_map, jenks_map, ncol = 3)









The broad geography is stable across the three views, but the boundaries between classes move. For a short exercise, I prefer the quantile version because it avoids giving most subzones the same pale colour; in a formal report I would also show the numeric class breaks.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1B: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation
section: Small multiples and a selected planning area
text:
Small multiples and a selected planning area
The three age groups can be compared as small multiples. I also map Tampines on its own because selecting a single planning area makes its internal variation easier to see.


Show R code
mpsz_long <- mpsz_pop |>
  select(SUBZONE_N, young, active, aged, geometry) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(young, active, aged), names_to = "cohort", values_to = "population")

tm_shape(mpsz_long) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "population",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 5, values = "BuGn"),
    col = "white",
    lwd = 0.1
  ) +
  tm_facets(by = "cohort", ncol = 3) +
  tm_title("Population cohorts by subzone, 2020") +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE)











Show R code
tampines <- mpsz_pop |> filter(PLN_AREA_N == "TAMPINES")

tm_shape(tampines) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "dependency",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 4, values = "YlGnBu"),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Dependency ratio"),
    col = "white"
  ) +
  tm_title("Dependency ratio within Tampines") +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE)

title: Hands-on Exercise 1B: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation
section: Complementing a map with a chart
text:
Complementing a map with a chart
The map answers where dependency is higher. The bar chart adds a quick comparison of the planning areas with the largest resident population, which is helpful because a high ratio in a small subzone and a high ratio in a large subzone do not imply the same service demand.


Show R code
planning_area_totals <- mpsz_pop |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  group_by(PLN_AREA_N) |>
  summarise(total = sum(total, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  slice_max(total, n = 10) |>
  arrange(total)

population_chart <- ggplot(planning_area_totals, aes(x = total / 1000, y = fct_reorder(PLN_AREA_N, total))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2a788e") +
  labs(title = "Largest planning areas by resident population", x = "Residents (thousands)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

map_for_composition <- ggplot(mpsz_pop) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = dependency), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.08) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "C", na.value = "grey90", name = "Dependency\nratio") +
  labs(title = "Dependency ratio, 2020") +
  theme_void()

map_for_composition + population_chart + plot_layout(widths = c(1.25, 1))

title: Hands-on Exercise 1B: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation
text:
Interactive version and submission image
The interactive map keeps the same measure but adds a popup for the subzone name, total population and dependency ratio. I also save the static map as a PNG so it can be submitted to eLearn as an image rather than a text-only URL.



Finished thematic map for eLearn submission




Show R code
tmap_mode("view")
tm_shape(mpsz_pop) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "dependency",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 5, values = "YlOrRd"),
    popup = c("SUBZONE_N", "total", "dependency"),
    id = "SUBZONE_N"
  )

title: Hands-on Exercise 1B: Thematic Mapping and GeoVisualisation
text:
Reflection
The two strongest lessons for me were practical rather than cosmetic. First, matching the CRS before buffering or overlaying is essential; a layer can look plausible on screen and still be wrong for distance-based work. Second, a choropleth is sensitive to classification choices. I found the map much easier to read after comparing the alternatives instead of treating the first colour scheme as the final answer.
